name: Crypto-Anarchism
summary: Crypto-anarchism holds that strong cryptography, anonymous networks and digital money will let individuals trade, speak and associate beyond the reach of states, weakening their power to tax, regulate and surveil and possibly causing their collapse. It is a technology-first, libertarian strand of anarchism, with markets and reputation expected to replace state coordination.
scope: The cypherpunk strand founded by Timothy C. May (The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto, 1988/1992; the Cyphernomicon, 1994), with Eric Hughes's Cypherpunk's Manifesto. It is libertarian and market-anarchist in orientation, not the social anarchism of the left. Later network-state ideas and Jim Bell's assassination politics are treated as offshoots and not as the mainstream.

keyFigures.name: Timothy C. May
keyFigures.role: Wrote the Crypto Anarchist Manifesto and the Cyphernomicon and is credited as founder of the movement.

sources.title: Crypto-anarchy
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Overview of the movement, its figures, its relation to libertarianism and anarcho-capitalism, and its stance on surveillance, markets and Bitcoin.

sources.title: The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto
sources.author: Timothy C. May
sources.usedFor: The founding text: anonymous transactions, reputations, weakened state control of taxation and regulation, collapse of barbed-wire property such as IP, and the admitted dangers of black markets and assassination markets.

sources.title: A Cypherpunk's Manifesto
sources.author: Eric Hughes
sources.usedFor: Privacy as the basis of an open society, anonymous transaction systems, encryption as private act, and building the tools oneself.

sources.title: The Cyphernomicon, section 16.5
sources.author: Timothy C. May
sources.usedFor: May's views on government as a threat to liberty, majority rule, voting, taxes, drug and gun laws, and an unwritten constitution of limits.

sources.title: The Cyphernomicon, section 16.4
sources.author: Timothy C. May
sources.usedFor: The manifesto as embedded in the Cyphernomicon: state response, markets for anything, effects on corporations and intellectual property.

sources.title: Timothy C. May
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: May as founder of the movement, his libertarian outlook, arms writing, and critical assessment of his views.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Crypto-anarchists want state power shrunk and funded services starved of tax revenue; a state-provided health system is not part of the program, inferred from the anti-state, anti-tax stance.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: A wage floor is a state regulation of economic activity that anonymous digital markets are expected to make unenforceable; inferred from May's anticipated end of regulation.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: May foresaw a liquid market for anything expressible in words and pictures and an anarcho-capitalist market system in place of state control.

public-ownership.rationale: Nothing in the movement favors state-owned industry; its aim is to remove state control of economic life through cryptographic means.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: May expected cryptography to undermine the state's power to tax, and he calls tax burdens already extreme; higher taxes run against the whole project.

unions-good.rationale: Crypto-anarchist texts say nothing on unions; adherents are mostly market-minded individualists but voluntary association is acceptable, so the answer is split.

property-fundamental.rationale: May's barbed-wire analogy treats technology as a way to secure holdings and exchanges against state override, though he also expects to dissolve intellectual property.

regulate-corporations.rationale: The manifesto expects anonymous networks to dissolve government regulation of economic activity, so adherents oppose, rather than want, more regulation.

cut-welfare.rationale: May lists welfare policy among state overreach and warns of unfunded welfare liabilities; adherents lean toward cutting it, though the texts do not argue the dependency claim.

worker-ownership.rationale: The movement is indifferent to ownership structure; voluntary cooperatives are as permissible as firms in a pseudonymous market, and no source takes a side.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Hughes holds that privacy is necessary for an open society and that governments will not grant it; mass surveillance is exactly what the movement exists to defeat.

legalize-drugs.rationale: May names drug enforcement as state overreach and expects drug dealers to use anonymous networks regardless; Silk Road was run in this spirit.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: The movement treats free, anonymous and pseudonymous speech as its central value and speech controls as what encryption is meant to defeat.

strong-leader.rationale: May states that governments of any stripe threaten individual freedom, so a leader with more power to bypass checks is the opposite of the aim.

state-harmful.rationale: May's manifesto and his 'smash the State' line, together with the claim that all governments threaten freedom, put the state's removal at the center of the movement.

limit-guns.rationale: May lists gun control among state overreach and wrote often of arming himself against government agents.

empower-police-military.rationale: Adherents seek to shrink state coercive capacity; more police and military authority runs against the aim of ungovernable private exchange.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Consensual exchange free from state interference, including black markets in anything, is the movement's stated direction; no source discusses sex work itself so this is inferred from that principle.

decide-locally.rationale: The movement wants decisions made by individuals and voluntary online groups, not by any territorial government; local government is not its preferred scale, so the answer is split.

rehabilitation.rationale: Criminal justice is not addressed; adherents want state penal power minimized but the texts offer no view on rehabilitation versus punishment.

traditional-family.rationale: The movement is silent on family structure and concerned with privacy; adherents range from socially conservative to liberal.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Not addressed; adherents want the state out of marriage, and would not oppose a legal option, so this is a weak lean from the privacy and freedom values.

abortion-legal.rationale: Not addressed; the emphasis on individual bodily and informational autonomy and distrust of state regulation suggests legality, but adherents are split.

more-religion-public.rationale: Religion in public life is not addressed; a movement built on voluntary private association has no place for state-promoted religion, which is an inference.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: State programs to redress historic injustice would require taxation and state action that adherents reject; the texts never discuss it.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Not a topic of the movement's texts, and adherents are split.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The movement treats cyberspace as a post-national space where identity is chosen and pseudonymous; it does not defend national culture, though it is not a focus.

gradual-change.rationale: May predicts abrupt change and the collapse of governments driven by technology rather than slow reform within institutions.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Borders matter little to a movement built on borderless networks, but the texts never discuss immigration, so this is an inference.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Hughes notes encryption restrictions stop at borders, and the movement rejects any supranational government as another state power.

free-trade.rationale: Freedom to trade is described as a core crypto-anarchist principle and May imagines anonymous worldwide commerce evading state barriers.

nation-first.rationale: Not addressed; the movement is cosmopolitan in practice but adherents include nationalists, so I do not infer a lean.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Any state military action is opposed as state power; the texts never discuss intervention, so this is inferred.

open-borders.rationale: Cyberspace sovereignty and free movement of money and people fit the movement, but the texts never address physical borders.

limit-growth.rationale: Environmental limits are not addressed; the movement is pro-technology and pro-trade and would resist state-imposed limits.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Not addressed; state-led action would conflict with the anti-state, anti-tax outlook, but adherents are mixed on the science.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The movement rests on the belief that cryptography and software will reshape society and power; May likens it to printing and barbed wire.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Not addressed; technophile adherents often favor nuclear energy but the movement does not take a stance.

revolution-justified.rationale: May's manifesto announces a specter haunting the world and expects the collapse of governments, though by technology rather than armed rising; Jim Bell's assassination politics is a fringe extreme.

experts-over-public.rationale: The movement trusts individual choice and distrusts authority including technocratic; the texts offer no explicit view.

central-planning.rationale: Central planning is state control of the economy, the opposite of the market anarchy May forecasts.

socialized-markets.rationale: Ownership form is a matter of indifference to the movement, so a market with worker-owned firms is permissible but not specifically endorsed.

land-value-tax.rationale: A tax replacing others is still a tax; adherents aim to erode the state's ability to tax and view taxation as extreme.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Taxation generally is what the manifesto expects crypto anarchy to undermine, and May calls tax burdens extreme.

basic-income.rationale: A state-run transfer funded by taxation is contrary to the movement's goal of ending state revenue; May also condemns welfare policy.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: May foresees anonymous trade that evades state border and economic controls; tariffs are one such control.

state-directs-investment.rationale: State direction of the economy is what anonymous markets are expected to dissolve.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The movement does not prescribe a distribution of property; it is indifferent so long as exchange is voluntary.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The movement is oriented to digital money and market exchange; Bitcoin is presented as its natural currency.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Digital cash outside state issuance is a central goal; Bitcoin is held up as suited to crypto-anarchy and May stresses currency export controls as overreach.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: State-recognized bodies that set wages and prices are a form of state economic control that the movement rejects.

one-party-rule.rationale: May says governments of any stripe threaten freedom and the movement aims to destroy state rule, so party rule is the opposite.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Hereditary rule is a form of government and so opposed; adherents reject the legitimacy of coercive rule rather than argue about its form.

democracy-best.rationale: May says majority rule can ignore minority rights and that politics does not secure lasting liberty, though he prefers democracy to worse systems.

direct-votes.rationale: May says too many decisions are put to a vote and that electronic democracy is worse, being faster and less considered.

workers-councils.rationale: A council-based political power is still a government and a collectivist one, and no crypto-anarchist source argues for it.

right-to-secede.rationale: The movement's thrust is that individuals and groups can exit state jurisdiction; later network-state ideas imagine online communities seceding into recognized sovereignty.

natural-rulers.rationale: A movement premised on abolishing rule rejects the idea that some are born to rule.

political-violence-never.rationale: The movement prefers technological means but does not renounce violence; May warns of assassination markets and Bell's proposal exists in the milieu.

war-builds-character.rationale: Not addressed; war is a state activity and the movement's emphasis on voluntary exchange makes it unlikely to endorse it.

separate-church-state.rationale: Not addressed; adherents want state power limited in every domain, which implies separation.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Imposing religious law is a form of state coercion that adherents reject.

private-courts-defense.rationale: May describes the end-state as anarcho-capitalist, in which private reputation systems and contracts replace state services.

military-superiority.rationale: Not addressed; the movement rejects state military power as part of its anti-state stance.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The movement stresses individual pseudonymous identity and voluntary association, not ethnic nationhood, though Finn Brunton notes May's own racist writings.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The movement is individualist and market-oriented; its historical analysis is about technology (printing, barbed wire), not class conflict.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Redistribution is a state act that adherents reject; reputation and market exchange produce unequal results by design.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Not addressed; adherents who favor property rights might support it but there is no documented position.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Reparations would be taxpayer-funded state transfers; the movement does not discuss them.

civilizational-union.rationale: Not addressed; a union of states would add state power, which adherents oppose.

self-interest-moral.rationale: May's reputation-driven, anonymous market order assumes people act for self-interest, and his libertarian roots treat that as legitimate.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The movement is organized around individual liberty and privacy rights against community and state claims.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: The cypherpunk texts concern privacy and money, not environmental ethics; no stance can be inferred.

limit-population.rationale: State population policy is coercive and not endorsed; no source discusses it.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The movement is technophile and builds on networks, computers and advanced mathematics.

accelerate-technology.rationale: May expects the technology to spread whatever institutions do and welcomes the disruption of regulation, guilds and corporations.

human-enhancement.rationale: Not addressed directly; the freedom ethos and the extropian overlap in the cypherpunk milieu favor it.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Cypherpunks favor code that protects individuals (smart contracts), not algorithmic government decisions, but the texts do not discuss algorithmic governance.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: This is the movement's defining demand; Hughes and May treat strong encryption as the foundation of privacy and of resistance to state power.

restore-past-order.rationale: The manifesto looks forward to a technology-driven transformation, not a restoration.

results-over-ideology.rationale: The movement is ideological and technological at once; no source takes a side, so adherents are split.

direct-action.rationale: Cypherpunks answer politics by writing and deploying code rather than by lobbying or elections, which is a form of direct action; Hughes says defend privacy ourselves.

means-match-ends.rationale: Hughes urges building the systems of privacy ourselves, so tools prefigure the society; the principle is not stated as such.

return-to-foraging.rationale: The movement depends on advanced computing and networks.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Information markets and reputation presuppose specialized exchange; May foresees a market for anything.

distribute-by-need.rationale: The movement's order is market exchange by voluntary trade, not distribution by need.

production-for-use.rationale: Profit and market exchange are expected to continue, though adherents would not force a choice of motives.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Adherents of the market anarchy May describes see profit as a legitimate return of voluntary exchange.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: A class dictatorship is a form of state rule, which the movement fundamentally rejects.

collective-farming.rationale: Compulsory collectivization is state coercion; no source supports it.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: The market-anarchist outlook sees states as the source of war; May describes the anarcho-capitalist system as the goal.

taxation-theft.rationale: May says crypto anarchy will weaken the state's power to tax and calls tax burdens extreme, but the sources do not call it theft in terms, so a lean rather than a forceful claim.

harm-principle.rationale: The movement permits any private transaction between consenting parties and rejects state restriction of consensual acts such as drug use; May also concedes harmful markets will arise.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The movement's logic concerns individual privacy and pseudonymous persons rather than group rights.

conscription.rationale: May lists many state coercions as overreach and the movement rejects compulsion by the state.

exit-over-voice.rationale: May holds that politics does not secure lasting liberty and that technology lets individuals escape state control, which is exit; network-state ideas formalize it.

state-as-business.rationale: The network-state idea of competing consensual jurisdictions fits customer exit, though the early texts do not frame it this way.

positive-liberty.rationale: The movement's liberty is freedom from interference, and its leading figures reject welfare policies and redistribution.

media-academia-power.rationale: Not addressed; adherents distrust elites but sources give no stance.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Brunton reports racist ideas in May's writings, but this is not a movement doctrine and most adherents reject or ignore it.

organic-representation.rationale: Representation through family and trade bodies is a form of corporatist state structure; the movement rejects state structures.

total-state.rationale: The movement exists to resist state control, and May says governments of any stripe threaten freedom.

national-rebirth.rationale: Nationalist renewal is foreign to the movement's post-national, technology-driven outlook.

territorial-expansion.rationale: State expansion is opposed along with all state power.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Rule by oath is a form of governance by force and hierarchy, opposed by the movement; reputation is voluntary and market-based instead.

bound-labor.rationale: Compulsory labor tied to land is coercion, opposed under the movement's voluntarism.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Cypherpunk thought treats mathematics and cryptography as neutral tools that work regardless of who holds power, but the texts don't state an epistemology.

universal-morality.rationale: Not addressed; the libertarian roots might suggest natural rights but sources give no position.

single-common-good.rationale: The movement emphasizes individual privacy and competing private interests and Hughes speaks of a social contract only for deploying privacy systems.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Not addressed; there is no movement position.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Citizenship and return rights are matters of state policy the texts never discuss.

revive-national-language.rationale: A state language program would be state action; the texts do not address it.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Mandated democratic control of firms would be a state regulation of business, which adherents reject.

school-vouchers.rationale: Adherents want the state out of education, and vouchers would be a market-leaning improvement, though many would prefer no public funding at all.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: May warns of unfunded pension and welfare liabilities and the state's financial strain; the question of stimulus itself is not discussed.

economic-freedom.rationale: Economic freedom through digital money and unregulated trade is one of the movement's named aims, alongside political freedom and privacy.

rule-by-example.rationale: Not addressed; adherents reject rule altogether so would reject a ruler's example as a basis.

national-self-determination.rationale: Adherents favor individual and group exit from states rather than national self-determination as such.

force-without-un.rationale: State military force abroad is opposed; the question of UN approval is not discussed.

reason-over-faith.rationale: The movement is mathematical and rationalist in tone but takes no stand on faith.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: The movement opposes welfare, so reserving it for citizens is a lesser issue, but adherents prefer less welfare for all.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Adherents want welfare cut, not conditioned; the sources do not discuss conditionality.

class-collaboration.rationale: The movement frames society as individuals and pseudonyms trading, not employers and workers as blocs; no position is documented.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Not addressed; adherents are not Futurists, though they welcome disruption of institutions such as guilds and regulation.

dominated-front.rationale: Not addressed; state blocs are not a movement concern.

workers-nation.rationale: A class or nation-based organization is irrelevant to a movement of individuals and pseudonyms.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Law-mandated roles are state coercion; adherents oppose such law.

ban-interest.rationale: Banning lending is a state restriction on consensual financial contracts; the movement wants financial freedom.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Law-mandated segregation is state coercion, opposed by the movement's core principle, notwithstanding racist writings by some members that Brunton cites.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The movement regards the state as an instrument of control over people, though its explanation is not Marxist in kind.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Not addressed; adherents would not favor state direction of energy either way.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Compelled assimilation would be state coercion, and the movement is cosmopolitan; the texts do not address it.

elite-replacement.rationale: The movement does not espouse replacement theories; it is a technology doctrine.

proportional-representation.rationale: Electoral systems are not addressed; adherents distrust the state and voting generally.

national-mission.rationale: Spreading a government form abroad contradicts the movement's anti-state stance.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Not addressed; adherents are individualist and tend to dismiss structural claims.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: May calls professional politicians a replacement for citizen legislators and treats governments as threats to liberty.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Eugenic state policy is state coercion over the individual, opposed by the movement.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Not addressed; adherents distrust security forces but the texts take no position on accountability measures.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Adherents aim for a stateless anarcho-capitalist order, so a minimal state is better than a large one but still short of the goal.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: State or social pressure on private relationships is rejected, and the movement stresses individual choice.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Not discussed explicitly; the individualist ethos supports equal rights, though Brunton reports racist writings by May.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A question internal to Marxist-Leninist debate; the movement has no position on it.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: No crypto-anarchist source discusses settler states or colonialism.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Not addressed; adherents prefer less state law, not uniformity or its absence.

restrict-conversion.rationale: A legal restriction on religious choice is state coercion.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Adherents oppose such state bans on consensual private activity.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Adherents want the state out of schooling, so this is not a live question.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A strengthened state is the opposite of the movement's goal.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Adherents favor consent in the form of voluntary contract, though they would deny that any government can satisfy it.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist aims are not part of a free-trade, borderless movement.

population-transfer.rationale: State-forced removal of people is coercion and contrary to the movement's principles.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: May hopes crypto anarchy will reduce physical coercion, but the movement is not a formal non-aggression doctrine and he concedes assassination markets may arise.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Market competition and reputation are central to the order May describes, though not stated as a theory of progress among peoples.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: The movement opposes state suppression of political activity.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Not discussed; the movement defines freedom as non-interference by the state.

separated-powers.rationale: Adherents distrust all branches of government; they favor dispersal of power but prefer to abolish rather than balance.

vanguard-party.rationale: A disciplined party leading a revolution is the opposite of a dispersed, pseudonymous, individualist movement.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Not stated; redistributive priorities conflict with the movement's anti-tax stance.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Not addressed; adherents oppose public housing but the policy question is outside the texts.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Not addressed; adherents oppose state labor law of any kind.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: The texts say nothing about demography or poverty causes; adherents are split.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Not addressed; the movement is cosmopolitan and treats identity as chosen, though Brunton reports racist elements in May's writing.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: The movement does not want offices at all; lottery selection is a reform within the state it rejects.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Adherents regard state emergency powers as a prime example of the overreach they seek to defeat; Hughes warns privacy won't be granted by the state.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: May foresees price and regulatory control becoming unenforceable and favors free markets.

party-controls-media.rationale: Government control of information is what the movement's tools for anonymous communication are meant to defeat.

party-commands-army.rationale: Party control of force is the opposite of the movement's anti-state aims.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: The movement does not support state citizenship barriers, but the texts do not discuss naturalization.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Not addressed; adherents want the state minimal, not specially paid.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: A movement of dispersed, pseudonymous individuals has no binding party structure; the Cypherpunks were an open mailing list.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Supranational unions add another level of state power, which adherents reject.

head-commands-forces.rationale: State command of force is opposed regardless of who holds it.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Church governance is a matter for voluntary religious groups in the movement's view; no stance is documented.

clerical-rule.rationale: Clerical rule is a form of coercive government and is rejected.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Not addressed; adherents oppose state wars but the working-class framing is not theirs.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Censorship is what anonymous, encrypted publication is meant to defeat.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Adherents distrust concentration of power in office; May criticizes professional politicians, but term rules are a reform they do not discuss.

recall-officials.rationale: Not addressed; adherents want to dismantle rather than reform the state.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Adherents oppose state military power and foreign entanglements, though the texts never discuss alliances.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Banning rental contracts is state coercion over private exchange.

people-in-arms.rationale: May wrote of arming himself against government agents, and gun control is listed as state overreach; a citizen militia replacing the army is not stated.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: The movement lives in cyberspace and says nothing about rural versus urban morality.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: State reunification is a national goal that the movement does not hold.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: The movement's founders were engineers and physicists; sources show no view on educated elites versus ordinary people.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Cultural comparison is outside the texts; adherents are divided, and Brunton reports racist ideas in May's writings that others do not share.

death-penalty.rationale: Adherents distrust state power over life, but the texts do not discuss capital punishment.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Adherents would rather the state did not run schooling, so they have no view on what state curricula contain.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Adherents want less state schooling; mandated creationism would be state imposition, but the texts do not address it.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Restrictions on information and sexual content are state censorship that the movement is built to evade.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Citizenship rules are not part of the movement; adherents prefer chosen membership.

minority-language-support.rationale: Not addressed; state-funded language programs conflict with anti-tax views.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Adherents want the state not to burden anyone, which favors exemptions, but the texts do not address them.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: The movement prizes pseudonymity and the freedom to live as one chooses, though it does not discuss social conformity.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Not addressed; adherents respect contracts but also distrust lenders backed by states.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Decolonization and national independence are not discussed in the movement's texts.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Not addressed; adherents reject writing new state constitutions as the way to liberty.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The movement puts political and economic freedom first and rejects trading them for state-led growth.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: State aid is funded by taxation, which adherents oppose.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: State nuclear arsenals are state power; adherents do not endorse them, but the texts do not discuss them.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Not addressed; adherents want no head of state but would prefer a weakly powered one.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Adherents want central banking replaced by private digital money, so a central bank with stable prices as its goal is not the aim.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Territorial disputes between states are not discussed by the movement.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: A common-good test would let the state override property; the movement's barbed-wire analogy values secure holdings.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: A dispute about the Soviet Union's character that the movement's texts never take up.

precautionary-principle.rationale: A state-enforced precautionary standard is a regulation the movement dislikes, but the texts do not address it.

collective-defense.rationale: State alliances are state power; adherents are not committed either way.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: International law on annexation is not discussed in the sources.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Adherents oppose extending state authority over any institution.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The movement wants no head of state, so the question of a symbolic one is not addressed.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Adherents favor exit from states and oppose coercion to keep regions in.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Autonomy and exit fit the movement, but the texts do not discuss it.

sacred-ruler.rationale: A sacred ruler is the antithesis of a movement that rejects rule.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Adherents want less taxation and not a particular scheme, so a flat tax is neither a goal nor rejected.

character-from-environment.rationale: The nature versus nurture question is not discussed in the sources.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Adherents say legitimate government is bounded by an unwritten constitution of limits, so unbound rulers are rejected.

space-expansion.rationale: The movement's technophile milieu favors it, but the texts do not mention space.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Not addressed; May's remarks on limits and checks are not a theory of mixed constitution.

leader-cult.rationale: State-led glorification of a leader is the opposite of the movement's individualist and anti-state outlook.

equal-parenting.rationale: Family-court presumptions are not discussed; adherents want less state involvement but no source says what follows.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A Maoist question the movement never addresses.

land-redistribution.rationale: Seizing property for redistribution contradicts secure property and opposition to state coercion.

refugee-return.rationale: The movement does not discuss refugees or return rights.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: State territorial claims are state power and not part of the movement.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Punishing leaving a religion is state coercion over private conscience.

women-must-cover.rationale: State dress mandates are coercion; the movement stands for individual choice.

common-currency.rationale: Adherents prefer private digital currencies over any state-issued currency, shared or not.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Not part of the movement; adherents oppose forming larger states.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Minority institutions within states are not discussed, as the movement is post-national.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Adherents favor exit over struggle within state structures, but the texts do not address minorities.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: May explains change through technology (printing, barbed wire), which is a technological rather than Marxian materialism.

ban-cartels.rationale: Adherents oppose state regulation of markets, and May says crypto will alter the power of corporations without state action.

no-bailouts.rationale: May warns of financial strain on the state and the movement is hostile to public money for private failures.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: May says majority rule can ignore minority rights, and thinks legitimate government has limits on itself.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: State mandates on composition are regulation that adherents reject.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: The movement is for free, anonymous worldwide trade.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: State-imposed standards on trade are regulation adherents oppose.

moral-incentives.rationale: Market exchange and reputation are the movement's incentive systems.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The movement relies on technology rather than armed groups, though Jim Bell's assassination politics is a fringe violent proposal.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Adherents oppose state-conferred privilege; inherited private wealth is a different matter and is not addressed.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Not addressed; state curricula are not a movement concern.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Adherents oppose rule over others as a matter of principle.

patriotic-education.rationale: State-led teaching of patriotism is state indoctrination, opposed by the movement.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Adherents reject state preferences of any sort, though the texts do not discuss this.

public-money-creation.rationale: Adherents want money issued outside state control; Bitcoin is the favored model.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Not addressed directly; May forecasts markets surviving and growing through technology.

former-empire-influence.rationale: State influence projection is not a movement aim.

delink-world-market.rationale: The movement stands for global trade and flows.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: A Leninist theory foreign to the movement; adherents do not see profits as extractive.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Freedom of association follows from the movement's libertarian roots, and May's writings on race are noted by Brunton, but the texts do not state this policy.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: May argues legitimate government has an unwritten constitution of limits and criticizes the view that law is whatever courts say; a written entrenched bill is a related but unstated step.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Colonial-era treaties are not a subject of the movement's texts.

elective-rulers.rationale: Adherents prefer no ruler; elections are not a solution in their view.

minority-veto.rationale: The movement's logic is that no decision should bind a non-consenting individual, close to a veto, but texts only say majority rule can ignore minorities.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: May's unwritten constitution of limits implies a right to resist rulers who exceed them, and his writing on arming against government agents is consistent.

parliament-supreme.rationale: May criticizes democratic expansion of government power; parliamentary supremacy would be the unbounded majority rule he distrusts.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Animal ethics is not addressed in any crypto-anarchist source.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Not addressed; no state-mandated standards would be endorsed either way.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Voluntary charity is acceptable but the movement states no duty.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: May says politics does not secure lasting liberty, and the movement answers with technology rather than participation; exit is its method.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: A Frankfurt-School thesis the cypherpunk texts do not take up.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: A Gramscian thesis on hegemony that the texts do not discuss.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: A dependency theory foreign to market-minded adherents.

native-born-offices.rationale: Offices are not the movement's concern and nativist restriction is not endorsed.

party-own-road.rationale: Relations among communist parties are not relevant to the movement.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Self-help and distrust of state aid fit, but the texts do not discuss development.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Irredentism is a state claim, not a movement aim.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Group-based political rank is opposed by an individualist, anti-state movement.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Adherents oppose fascist states but also reject constitutional mandates of this kind; the texts do not discuss it.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: May says governments of any stripe threaten freedom, which is in line with this equivalence, though not stated for these two regimes.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: US historiography is not a topic of the movement's sources.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Monument policy is not discussed; there is no documented position.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: The sources have no discussion of gendered public programmes.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: The sources do not discuss domestic violence services.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Not addressed; the movement is universalist about technology.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Military political power is state power the movement rejects.

paid-care-work.rationale: State payment for care work would be funded by taxation and is not endorsed.

filial-duty.rationale: Family obligations are not discussed in the movement's texts.

office-by-exam.rationale: Not addressed; adherents do not want offices.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: State restrictions on trade and investment are regulation adherents oppose.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Not addressed; the freedom ethos suggests agreeing, but the question concerns state marriage law.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Not addressed; adherents want less rather than more binding representation.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: May warns of unfunded state pension liabilities, and privately held savings fit the movement better than state pay-as-you-go.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Use-based tenure contradicts the secure property that the barbed-wire analogy values.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Adherents want to starve the state of revenue, so legislative budget control is a side issue with no documented view.

single-official-language.rationale: A mandated state language is coercion that adherents oppose, an inference from their anti-state principle since the texts never discuss it.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: A state ban on land sales to foreigners is a restriction on free trade.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: State anti-discrimination enforcement is regulation adherents oppose.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Adherents are market-minded and see consumption as voluntary exchange, though the texts do not discuss it.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: State covert warfare is state power, but the texts do not address it.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: State military coercion is opposed in all forms.

corporate-influence.rationale: Adherents dislike state-corporate entanglement as part of state overreach but would not regulate lobbying, so split.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: State restrictions on flows of money and information are what the movement seeks to defeat.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Tax-funded incentives for family policy are state action opposed by adherents.

residents-only-property.rationale: Restrictions on purchase conflict with free trade, though local control has some appeal.

job-guarantee.rationale: A state employment program is state economic direction funded by taxes.

democratic-peace.rationale: International relations theory is not discussed; adherents would see states as the source of war regardless of type.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The movement is anarchist and its tools are meant to make state law unenforceable; adherents do not grant the state authority.

non-intervention.rationale: Adherents oppose state intervention but also do not oppose private actors; no stance on the absolute claim.

industrial-unions.rationale: Union structure is not discussed in the sources.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Not part of the movement, which treats the state as the adversary.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Adherents want the state out of private contracts, so state marriage benefits are unwelcome, but this is not stated.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Adherents favor citizens' privacy but state secrecy is distrusted; Hughes says privacy is not secrecy, and May says state secrets could be traded.

local-production.rationale: Adherents want global anonymous trade, so a preference for local production is not part of their view.

informal-organisation.rationale: The Cypherpunks organized as an informal list, and pseudonymous groups without permanent structure are the movement's pattern.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Adherents reject the authority of both national and international law, so the ranking is moot.

religious-nation.rationale: Religious definition of a nation is a state matter foreign to the movement.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Ritual submission of states to a hegemon is a state hierarchy adherents reject, inferred from their anti-state stance.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Less transfer between regions is closer to less taxation, but the texts do not discuss it.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Private personal belongings are consistent, though the framing is Marxian and adherents also favor private means of production.

defeat-communism.rationale: Adherents oppose communism's state but the question is about foreign policy, on which the texts say nothing.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Adherents prefer fully private provision to publicly funded systems.

religion-illusion.rationale: The movement is silent on religion and its adherents include believers and atheists.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: May presents market exchange powered by technology as the path forward.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Adherents are market-minded and expect no systemic economic transformation, but the texts say nothing on women's equality.

socialized-care.rationale: Tax-funded public care is state provision that adherents oppose, inferred from their anti-tax stance.

purge-loanwords.rationale: State language policing is coercion that adherents oppose; the texts never discuss it.

treaties-binding.rationale: Treaties between states and nations are outside the movement's texts.

majority-settlement.rationale: State-driven settlement policy is coercion, opposed.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Adherents expect capitalist markets to continue and flourish in anarchic form.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Historic claims to land are not discussed in the movement's sources.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Not a movement doctrine; I infer rejection from its rationalist, evidence-based tone, though the texts are silent.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Criminalizing private consensual acts is state intrusion into private life, the opposite of the movement's principle.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Suppressing dissent is state coercion and information control, which cryptographic tools defeat.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Punishing speech is the state censorship the movement opposes.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: State domination of other peoples is contrary to anti-state principles, though the texts never discuss colonies.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: A religious doctrine the movement never discusses; adherents oppose state wars.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Religious political violence has no place in the movement.

participatory-democracy.rationale: May says too many decisions are put to a vote and criticizes electronic democracy, though voluntary self-governing groups online are acceptable.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: The movement does not use this framework and sources give no view.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Not addressed; adherents favor freedom of identity (pseudonymity) but a state legal regime is a separate matter.

assisted-dying.rationale: Individual autonomy implies agreement, but the texts do not discuss it.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: The movement stands outside left and right, and the Wikipedia article notes tensions between it and social anarchism.

alienated-labor.rationale: A Marxian concept absent from the movement's texts; market-minded adherents are unlikely to accept it.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Not part of the movement and the texts say nothing about it.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Adherents reject ruler authority of any kind.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Adherents want the state to restrict no one's dress, but the movement says nothing on state institutions' rules.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: State limits on private contracts are generally opposed, but the topic is not addressed.

social-market-economy.rationale: Adherents want market anarchy rather than a regulated social market.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Adherents want to end state forces, but the texts do not discuss a standing army and favor private defense.

rich-first.rationale: Development strategy is not addressed in the movement's texts.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Adherents oppose state military entanglements, but the texts are silent.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Hereditary succession of rulers is rejected as rule.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Adherents prefer free-market finance, but voluntary mutual credit is permissible.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: IMF conditionality is not discussed; adherents like austerity of state spending but distrust international lenders.

property-franchise.rationale: Adherents distrust voting itself, and do not seek to restrict a franchise.

domination-women-nature.rationale: An ecofeminist thesis that the cypherpunk texts do not address.

reification.rationale: A Marxian concept the cypherpunk texts never use.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Anonymous publishing makes publishing cheap for anyone, so the claim that the wealthy control it is not shared.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: May says legitimate government is bounded by limits and criticizes the view that law is whatever the courts decide.

racial-franchise.rationale: Adherents distrust voting and do not seek to restrict the franchise by race.

online-participation.rationale: Online deliberation fits the movement, but May warns against electronic democracy as hasty and distant from representation, so only weakly.

open-government-data.rationale: Adherents want transparency of state and privacy of individuals; the texts do not state it.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: State restriction on private relationships is opposed.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Voluntary boycott is free association, but the movement does not promote it.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Not addressed; adherents distrust state processes but would not oppose deliberation.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Religious reform is a matter for believers; the movement has no stance.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Adherents locate danger in the state rather than in wealth; May says barbed-wire style property is liberating.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Not addressed; adherents oppose state militaries.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: State promotion of any belief system is coercion that adherents oppose, an inference from anti-state principles.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Adherents want private enforcement and reputation, and do not endorse the state's police, but the texts do not explicitly discuss abolishing prisons.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Constitutional design for divided societies is not addressed.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Adherents oppose state welfare and favor voluntary or private help, though the texts do not argue effectiveness.

term-limits.rationale: Not addressed; adherents distrust professional politicians (May) but prefer abolition.

vote-delegation.rationale: Not addressed; the movement's liquid democracy overlap is not a documented position.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Not addressed; state policy priority is not their concern.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Internal rules of religious bodies are not addressed.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Authority within marriage is a private matter the texts do not discuss.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Local franchise rules are not discussed; adherents distrust voting in general.

rent-control.rationale: A price cap is the economic regulation that the movement expects markets to defeat.

abolish-ip.rationale: May's manifesto expects cryptography to dismantle the barbed wire around intellectual property.

uniformed-youth.rationale: State drilled youth movements are state indoctrination, opposed.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Nuclear basing is not discussed in the movement's texts.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Adherents oppose state military presence, but the texts do not address it.

recognise-genocide.rationale: State recognition of historical atrocities is not discussed.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Adherents see returns to property as legitimate in a market.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: May wrote of arming himself, and gun control is listed as state overreach, so self-defense is accepted.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Not a part of the movement's post-national outlook.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: A theoretical question in gender studies the movement does not address.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Feminist theory is not discussed in the movement's sources.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: A state cult of martyrs is foreign to the movement.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The movement is technical and pragmatic in tone.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Diaspora nationalism is not part of the movement.

culture-before-state.rationale: Nation-building strategy is not part of the movement.

god-not-male.rationale: Religious language is not discussed in the movement's texts.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Feminist theology is not discussed by the movement.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: State economic preference for an ethnic majority is regulation and discrimination the movement does not endorse.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Redrawing administrative regions is state action outside the movement's aims.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Voluntary communes are permitted in a free-association order but the movement does not prescribe them, and its market emphasis points the other way.

anonymous-payments.rationale: May's manifesto expects anonymous digital transactions to undermine state control of taxation and economic activity, and Hughes calls for anonymous transaction systems.

online-anonymity.rationale: The manifesto expects digital pseudonyms and reputations to replace identity, and Hughes says people should reveal their identity only by choice.

independent-unions.rationale: Inferred from market-anarchist voluntary association; unions would answer to members, not any state.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Inferred from the libertarian view that state ownership is not socialism worth the name and markets replace state coordination.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Crypto-anarchists expect markets and reputation to replace state provision.

second-chamber.rationale: Inferred: the aim is to weaken states, so further legislative bodies are not valued.

municipal-property.rationale: Inferred from the market-anarchist preference for private property and voluntary exchange.

confederal-coordination.rationale: The sources do not address assemblies; voluntary coordination is welcomed but not in this form.

family-wage.rationale: Inferred from reliance on markets and reputation to set pay.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Inferred from the libertarian view against state regulation; the sources do not discuss drugs.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Inferred: the strand is interested in life extension, but opposes state funding.

person-over-state.rationale: Hughes and May argue that privacy lets individuals protect themselves from the state and trade beyond its reach.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The sources do not address this; the strand is technology-first and neither promotes nor opposes spirituality.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Inferred: crypto-anarchists reject state authority, so powers a central legislature can withdraw are not valued.

gm-crops.rationale: Inferred from technological optimism and opposition to regulation.

dense-cities.rationale: The sources do not address urban form.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Inferred from the individualist, voluntarist framing, where individuals deal without regard to group identity.

racial-pride.rationale: The sources do not address this.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Inferred from the aim of weakening the state's power; force is for defence.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Crypto-anarchy aims at individuals and voluntary networks beyond states, so national identity is not a unit it cares about; inferred from the manifesto's anti-state stance.

communal-electorates.rationale: Reserved electorates assume state representation by community, which is the opposite of the stateless, voluntary association crypto-anarchists want; inferred.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: The ideology treats states as obsolete rather than as national bodies to defend, so it does not share nationalist partition fears; inferred.

free-public-college.rationale: Free tuition means state spending funded by taxation, which crypto-anarchism seeks to starve; inferred.

pollution-taxes.rationale: A pollution tax is a state levy; adherents would prefer property-rights and market solutions; inferred.

future-generations.rationale: The sources do not address environmental stewardship, and market-anarchists are divided on it.

women-distinct-values.rationale: The market-individualist outlook has no place for group-based claims about public life; inferred.

arms-reduction.rationale: Crypto-anarchists want states weakened, and state militaries with them; inferred, not stated in the sources.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Cypherpunks demand transparency from governments while defending private privacy; inferred from the privacy-for-individuals framing.

capital-controls.rationale: The manifesto says strong cryptography lets money and capital move beyond state reach, undermining the state's ability to control and tax it.

missingStatements.text: People should be able to send and receive money without the government being able to trace or block it.
missingStatements.rationale: May's manifesto expects anonymous digital transactions to undermine state control of taxation and economic activity, and Hughes calls for anonymous transaction systems.

missingStatements.text: People should be free to take part online anonymously or under pseudonyms without having to reveal their legal identity.
missingStatements.rationale: The manifesto expects digital pseudonyms and reputations to replace identity, and Hughes says people should reveal their identity only by choice.

missingStatements.text: Reputation among private parties, not legal identity or government licensing, should be the basis of trust in commerce.
missingStatements.rationale: May says reputations will be of central importance in dealings, far more than credit ratings, replacing state-backed identity.
missingStatements.declined: Niche and tied to crypto-anarchist market theory; trust by reputation is not a question other ideologies would split on in the test.

notes: Adherents are split on violence: Jim Bell's assassination politics and May's remarks on assassination markets sit at one end, while most cypherpunks stress privacy tools. Finn Brunton, cited in Wikipedia, finds racist ideas in some of May's writing; these are not treated as movement doctrine. Many answers outside privacy, money and state power are low-confidence inferences from the anti-state, market-anarchist core.
